title: Same pendulum, bigger swing. Does it take longer? Yes: 2.0 s a swing at 10 degrees, 2.5 s at 103.
description:
Same pendulum, bigger swing. Does it take longer? One simple pendulum (a point bob on a massless rod, length 0.9898 m, g = 9.80665 m/s^2) drawn twice at the same scale and released from rest at the same instant: the top panel from 10 degrees, the bottom panel from 103.415 degrees, 13.4 degrees above horizontal. The length is chosen so that the 10 degree swing takes exactly 2.000 s out and back, and the big angle is solved so that its swing takes exactly 2.500 s, from T = 4 sqrt(L / g) K(sin(theta0 / 2)) with K the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. RK4 at 3,600 steps per second; deterministic, no seed. Played at real speed. The counter in each panel shows the swing in progress and the strip between the panels ticks at the start of every swing.

Measured:
- closed form: K(sin 5 deg) = 1.573792; L = g (2.000 / 4 K)^2 = 0.989842 m; the small-angle period 2 pi sqrt(L / g) = 1.996193 s, so 10 degrees already runs 0.19 percent slow; the big angle solves to 103.415 degrees (k = sin 51.707 deg = 0.784857, K = 1.967240, 4 sqrt(L / g) K = 2.500000 s); T / T0 = (2 / pi) K = 1.252384 and T(103.415) / T(10) = 1.2500 exactly
- 10 degrees: every swing 2.000000 s out and back (RK4, closed form 2.000000); 20 swings in 40.000 s with the last turnaround at 40.000000 s; 40 bottom crossings, the first at 0.500 s and then every 1.000 s; speed at the bottom 0.5431 m/s (closed form sqrt(2 g L (1 - cos theta0)) = 0.5431); energy drift 4.8e-14
- 103.415 degrees: every swing 2.500000 s (closed form 2.500000); 16 swings in 40.000 s with the last turnaround at 40.000000 s; 32 bottom crossings, the first at 0.625 s and then every 1.250 s; speed at the bottom 4.8906 m/s (closed form 4.8906); the bob rises 22.96 cm above the pivot at each turnaround and spends 0.879 s of every swing above horizontal and 0.760 s within 10 degrees of a turnaround (30.4 percent of the time on 19.3 percent of the arc); energy drift 2.0e-14
- the same pendulum at other angles, T / T0: 30 degrees 1.0174 (2.031 s), 45 degrees 1.0400 (2.076 s), 60 degrees 1.0732 (2.142 s), 90 degrees 1.1803 (2.356 s, 18.0 percent slow), 120 degrees 1.3729 (2.741 s), 150 degrees 1.7622 (3.518 s, 76.2 percent slow), 170 degrees 2.4394 (4.869 s), 179 degrees 3.9011 (7.787 s)
- drift: the small swing gains 0.500 s a swing, a quarter swing every big swing; both bobs are at a turnaround together every 5 s (at 5, 15, 25 and 35 s on opposite sides, at 10, 20, 30 and 40 s both on the release side, 5 small swings to 4 big ones), so the counters read 6 and 5 at 10 s, 11 and 9 at 20 s, 16 and 13 at 30 s and 20 and 16 at 40 s
- checks: at half the time step (7,200 steps per second) the periods are unchanged to 1e-14 and the counts are 20 and 16; the video's last frame equals its first

Why: the push back toward the bottom is gravity's part along the arc, and it grows with the angle only as the sine of the angle, not the angle itself. At small angles the sine is almost the angle, so a wider swing gets a proportionally bigger push and the time per swing hardly changes: that is Galileo's rule, and it is 0.2 percent off at 10 degrees. Past 90 degrees the push stops growing and shrinks again, so the big bob is pushed back less than the straight-line rule would give: it climbs high, almost stops, and lingers near the top of every swing. Those slow ends are where the extra half second goes, and they get longer the higher you start: 18 percent at 90 degrees, 76 percent at 150, almost four times at 179.

Rerun sims/bigswing/bigswing.py with projects/bigswing/manifest.json and you get these numbers exactly.
